title: vLLM & the Serving Engine Landscape
desc: A pragmatic survey of the inference engines you'll actually choose between in production — vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, and the lightweight edge options — and a decision framework for picking one.
content:
Why You Can't Just Call model.generate()

Every LLMOps engineer eventually asks: why not just load the model in Hugging Face Transformers and call generate() in a loop? The answer is GPU utilization. Naive serving processes one request at a time (or small static batches), leaves the GPU idle between token steps, and re-allocates a worst-case-sized KV cache buffer per request. Measured utilization on plain transformers serving is typically 5-15%; a proper inference engine gets you to 60-80%+ by solving three problems at once: continuous batching (new requests join a running batch instead of waiting for it to finish), paged/managed KV cache (memory allocated in small blocks on demand instead of one huge contiguous buffer), and fused, hand-tuned CUDA kernels for attention and the MLP.

vLLM TGI TensorRT-LLM SGLang Ollama llama.cpp
📄
This lesson picks up from Day 1
You now know how to estimate KV cache size and required throughput. This lesson is about which engine turns those numbers into a running server. Day 3 is the hands-on EC2 deployment of the engine you pick here.
Static batching waits for the whole batch to finish before starting new requests. Continuous batching evicts a finished sequence (C) and admits a queued one (D) at the very next decode step — no request waits behind a slower sibling.

vLLM — The Default Choice

vLLM is open source, has an OpenAI-compatible API out of the box, and supports 100+ model architectures. Its core innovation, PagedAttention, allocates the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default) instead of one contiguous worst-case buffer, cutting memory fragmentation from ~60% to under 4%. Combined with continuous batching and automatic prefix caching, it is the right starting point for almost every team.

  • OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint — drop-in replacement for existing client code
  • Automatic prefix caching — free throughput when requests share a system prompt
  • Broadest hardware support: NVIDIA, AMD ROCm, Intel Gaudi, TPU (experimental)
  • Largest community — fastest to get a new open-weight model running day-of-release

Text Generation Inference (TGI)

TGI is Hugging Face's own serving engine, used internally for the Inference Endpoints product. It supports continuous batching, Flash Attention, and tensor parallelism much like vLLM, and integrates tightly with the Hugging Face Hub (private model auth, gated repos) if that's already your model registry.

⚠️
TGI is now in maintenance mode
Hugging Face's own TGI repository states it is in maintenance mode: the team now only accepts minor bug fixes and documentation PRs, and explicitly recommends vLLM, SGLang, or llama.cpp/MLX for new deployments. Treat TGI as a legacy option — fine to keep operating if you're already on it, but not where a new deployment should start in 2026.
vLLM
  • Fastest-moving, most model day-0 support
  • Best throughput on most published benchmarks
  • Prefix caching + PagedAttention out of the box
TGI
  • Tight Hugging Face Hub / gated-model integration
  • Mature guardrails: watermarking, token streaming, safety hooks
  • In maintenance mode — HF recommends vLLM/SGLang instead for new builds

TensorRT-LLM — Squeezing the Last 20%

TensorRT-LLM compiles your model into a NVIDIA-specific engine (.plan file). That compilation step costs you minutes of build time and operational complexity, but buys the best FP8/INT8 kernel performance available on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs. Reach for it only after you've measured that vLLM is the bottleneck and you can afford NVIDIA-only lock-in plus a heavier CI/CD story (rebuild the engine on every model or driver change).

SGLang — Structured Output & Multi-Call Programs

SGLang, from the LMSYS team behind Chatbot Arena, uses RadixAttention — a radix tree that shares KV cache across requests more aggressively than vLLM's block table. It shines when your workload is JSON-schema-constrained generation or chains several LLM calls per user request (agents, multi-step extraction) — its structured decoding is measurably faster than grammar libraries bolted onto other engines.

Ollama & llama.cpp — When You Don't Need a Cluster

Ollama (built on llama.cpp) is not a production multi-tenant server — it has no continuous batching worth mentioning and is CPU/single-GPU-workstation oriented. But it is the fastest path from "I have a GGUF file" to "I have a local endpoint," and is the right tool for local development, prototyping prompts, and genuinely single-user edge deployments (on-device, air-gapped).

Shell · minimal server launch, three engines side by side
# vLLM — OpenAI-compatible server, one command (current CLI)
pip install vllm
vllm serve meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --port 8000
# older versions: python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model ... --port 8000

# TGI — via the official Docker image (maintenance mode; shown for completeness)
docker run --gpus all -p 8080:80 -v $PWD/data:/data \
  ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:latest \
  --model-id meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct

# Ollama — local dev, single command, no Docker
ollama run llama3.1:8b

Engine Decision Framework

If your situation is…Reach for
Standard chat/completion API, want it running todayvLLM
Already deep in the Hugging Face Hub ecosystem, private/gated modelsTGI (legacy — vLLM now covers gated-model auth too)
Measured vLLM as the bottleneck, all-NVIDIA fleet, can own a compile stepTensorRT-LLM
Heavy structured/JSON output or multi-call agent programsSGLang
Local dev laptop, prototyping, single-user edge deviceOllama / llama.cpp
🔑
Key Takeaways
1. Any dedicated engine beats naive generate() serving by 5-10x GPU utilization via continuous batching + paged KV cache. 2. vLLM is the correct default — broadest support, OpenAI-compatible API, biggest community. 3. TGI is now in Hugging Face's own maintenance mode — don't start a new deployment on it; move to TensorRT-LLM for the last 20% on NVIDIA-only fleets, or SGLang for structured/agentic workloads. 4. Ollama/llama.cpp are dev and edge tools, not multi-tenant production servers.

1. Your team serves a standard chat API, has no NVIDIA-only constraint, and wants day-of-release support for new open-weight models. Which engine should you reach for first?
2. What problem does PagedAttention specifically solve?
3. Your workload chains 4 LLM calls per user request and needs strict JSON-schema-constrained output on every call. Which engine is purpose-built for this?
